4 . if the stock is sold at a loss , it can be used to offset other capital gains or up to $ 3,000 of ordinary income .

fyi - the 90 's are over
by rich karlgard 01.03.01 , 6 : 00 am et

if you think the stock market is a mess now , wait until the tens of thousands of newly minted millionaires from the 1990s realize they blew it .

what 's the difference between today 's stock market and the tulip frenzy of 17th century holland .  tulip mania , for all its excesses , didn 't make anyone rich .  the dot - com bubble , on the other hand , has anointed tens of thousands of new millionaires .  the big difference : the tulip bubble popped and that was it .  the dot - com bubble is a dud but there is still time to cash in your chips -- if you act fast .

the point here is that the 1990s are over and it 's time to get back to basics .  over the next few months forbes will be publishing a series of articles about how to manage your money in the new millennium .  here are the highlights : 
- be a contrarian .  the best way to beat the market is to go where the crowd is not .  this means selling growth stocks and buying value .  over the last ten years , growth stocks soared 13 % a year , value stocks 10 % .  these days you can get value stocks at a 40 % discount to growth stocks , the biggest gap in 15 years .  this means you can buy the likes of boeing , exxon , shell and merck at the same p / e as youd pay for a startup .  if you 're in the mutual fund business , buy wellesley income and dodge & cox stock .  if you 're an individual investor , buy the stocks at the end of the value 500 list ( pg . 180 of the dec . 18 issue of forbes ) .  they 're cheap .
- forget about market timing .  the great sin of the 1990s is that the vast majority of investors thought they were smarter than the market .  they were not .  the best way to invest is the simplest way : dollar - cost - averaging .  that is , put a fixed sum of money into a mutual fund every month .  over time , your cost basis will be lower than the market price .  if you 're nearing retirement and have a huge chunk of your net worth tied up in stocks , you should take some money off the table .  but if you 're younger , you are still better off investing regularly in a good mutual fund .  you 'll be able to buy more shares when the market dips .  market timers are kidding themselves .  the evidence is clear : over a ten - year period , they underperform buy - and - hold investors by 4.5 % a year .
- focus on asset allocation .  the most important thing you can do is make sure your portfolio is properly allocated .  that is , determine how much of your money should be in stocks and how much in bonds and cash .  the easiest way to do this is to determine what percentage of your portfolio should be in stocks by subtracting your age from 100 .  so if you 're 30 , 70 % of your assets should be in stocks .  if you 're 60 , 40 % should be in stocks .  if you 're 80 , 20 % should be in stocks .  then divide your stock allocation among large - cap , small - cap , international and emerging market stocks .  the rest should go into bonds and cash .
- keep your costs down .  the only thing you can control about your portfolio is the costs .  these include commissions , fees and taxes .  pay attention to all of them .  the average mutual fund charges an annual fee of 1.5 % .  that 's too high .  the vanguard 500 index fund charges .2 % .
